checks.method: Reconstructed Section 4.2 using two distinct completions and partitioned their two-element A-edges into intersection sizes zero, one and two when their B-edges are disjoint. Checked the stated sunflower witness in each case.
checks.observation: The three cases are exhaustive: zero gives an empty-core sunflower with R; two uses the x-star corresponding to the common A-edge; one chooses a design triple through the common point avoiding the two other endpoints, possible since 5 > 2+2. Disjoint component supports ensure the stated intersections. The symmetric argument yields intersecting coordinate-edge families, and the five-cycle bound gives at most four completion pairs.
checks.scope: Completeness of the split-completion argument as written

checks.method: Tested whether the weighted-pair paragraph proves a common point rather than merely pairwise intersections. Traced the nonempty hypothesis, integer pigeonhole step, and total-weight contradiction.
checks.observation: A selected pair of weight at least nine contains a point of weight at least five. Any other admissible pair omitting that point would force total weight at least fourteen, exceeding ten. This supplies a single point common to every used extension pair, supporting the injection into five triples; the nonempty and nonnegative hypotheses are now explicit.
checks.scope: Common-point conclusion versus a weaker pairwise-intersection interpretation

checks.method: Compared Sections 3 and 6 against the frozen Python and C++ diagnostic summaries, and traced whether any diagnostic count enters the incidence derivation.
checks.observation: The proof reaches 37m ≤ 1512 using actual-family trace and degree bounds only. The diagnostic records maximum five among enumerated candidate geometries and explicitly requires a normalization theorem; no such finite-coverage premise appears in the structural proof. The manuscript correctly declines the universal45 conclusion. The separate opening sentence of Section 6 nevertheless needs the limited scope stated in my required revision.

Fixing one coordinate and using all five opposite edges gives five pairwise-intersecting completions, exposing why the shared-star hypotheses matter. The computation is a local diagnostic only, not a universal normalization argument.

checks.method: Reconstruct Section 3.1 using arbitrary actual R and y-star member S; inspect ProfileAOutside.disjoint_rows_outside_sum_le_two and the previously inspected TwoStarResidual theorem.
checks.observation: If R has at most two U-points, it has at least two outside U. Independence gives y outside U, x absent from S, and y absent from R. Under the hypothetical disjointness R∩S=∅ these outside points are distinct, so their union has at least three points outside U, contradicting the bound two. Every y-link triple therefore meets R, producing a four-point transversal in conflict with minimum size six. No bound on the ambient support or assumption R⊆U∪V is used.
checks.scope: Residual-support lemma and possible center/outside overlap loopholes

checks.method: Recompute meeting bounds and enumerate all nonnegative integer census triples satisfying total 61, outsider incidence 76 and n2≤27; then apply the actual disjoint-completion lower bound. Read the corresponding ProfileACounts and ProfileAOutside statements.
checks.observation: The general meeting bound is 57, so every row has a disjoint partner. For a two-outsider row the degree sum is at most 66 and the closed meeting neighborhood is at most 52, leaving at least nine distinct disjoint members. The outside-sum inequality forces each completion into H0. Before this step census gives n2=n0+15≥15, so selecting such a row is justified. The surviving triples are (n0,n1,n2)=(9,28,24),(10,26,25),(11,24,26),(12,22,27).
checks.scope: Nine-completion lower bound, nonemptiness and sharp integer margins

checks.method: Test the rival possibility of an A-key row and a B-key row coexisting; read TwoSideConcentration.concentrate_from_disjoint_completion_types and track the same fixed supports A,B from Section 4.
checks.observation: The former row has at least nine H0 completions with A-trace size one; the latter has at least nine with A-trace size three. Even if completions are otherwise reused across rows, these two chosen completion families are disjoint because a single set cannot have both trace sizes. Their union would have at least eighteen members inside H0 of size at most twelve. The argument does not need the two original rows themselves to be disjoint. Synchronizing A,B once removes any relabeling loophole.

Two extensions of a single B triple, with different A points, and its x-star member are three distinct sets with exactly that triple as common intersection; hence W has at most ten members.

checks.observation: A selected heavy pair has a point of weight at least five. Any heavy pair omitting it would give at least 14 total units, contradiction. Equal extension pairs and multiple high-weight points do not invalidate this argument. The common point lies outside each key; deleting it recovers that key, proving injection into five blocks. Exact enumeration found maximum five heavy keys and no empty common intersection. Each fixed-key outsider graph has at most four edges by the maximum-degree-two condition on four vertices, yielding n2 at most 20.

The bound comes from an x-star member disjoint from two nonempty four-sets, hence three distinct petals. If every y-star member instead meets R, deleting y preserves the meeting because y∉R, making the four-set R a transversal of a link whose transversal number is six. No ambient support bound is assumed.

checks.method: Checked the set inclusion and double-counting identities in TwoHighIncidence and MeetingDefect, and read inherited singleton_intersection_card_le_forty and meeting_incidence_singleton_defect. Enumerated all 25 pairs of traces of size at least three on a fixed four-set.
checks.observation: The trace union is contained in the anchor four-set, so its intersection has at least two points; the finite check reaches minimum two. In the meeting sum singleton traces contribute one, all other nonempty traces at least two, and the unique anchor contributes four. Thus adding the singleton total to the degree sum gives at least 2|M|+2. The formal lemma requires and uses R∈H, so the excess is not applied to an external anchor.

checks.method: Read CompletionCompatibility, its ProfileASplit caller and the three-case prose construction in Section 4.2. Checked the center and anchor memberships and projection reconstruction.
checks.observation: Distinct completions cannot be disjoint because together with their common disjoint nonempty anchor they would form an empty-core sunflower. If one coordinate pair is disjoint and the other overlaps, the chosen design triple has the exact common trace; adjoining x gives a member distinct from both completions because both omit x. Equal completions are treated separately by the nonempty two-point projections. Projection pairs determine the completion, so the 2×2 product bound counts actual members injectively.
checks.scope: Split-completion compatibility and quantification over equal versus distinct completions

checks.method: Read GenericHeavyExtensions and Section 4.3; checked the mass argument algebraically and independently enumerated all 8008 nonnegative integer six-point weight vectors of total at most ten.
checks.observation: Each nonempty heavy pair has an endpoint of weight at least five. A heavy pair omitting that endpoint would require at least fourteen total units. Of the 8008 vectors, 687 admit heavy pairs; all of their complete collections of pairs of weight at least nine have a common point. This is a bounded diagnostic supplement to the direct proof. The proof does not assume distinct keys have distinct extension pairs. It injects keys into triples by adjoining the common point, which lies outside every key and can therefore be erased to recover that key.
checks.scope: Common-extension concentration, nonemptiness and injectivity

committed_findings.summary: The core structural implications survive a direct quantifier and distinctness audit. The residual-transversal contradiction uses three genuinely distinct members; the meeting excess counts the anchor because it is in the closed neighborhood; split-completion sunflower constructions have a distinct star member through the omitted center. The common-extension argument needs no injectivity of the extension-pair map, and its final key-to-triple map is injective because the common point is outside every key. No counterexample or required repair was found.

Distinct residual completions are required for the sunflower contradiction; x is absent from both, so the constructed star member is distinct. If both coordinates are disjoint, R is disjoint from both completions, giving three distinct petals. Coordinate images jointly determine a completion, justifying the product bound.
